What I heardFrom Richard Ladson · notes from our conversation

For Sherene Woolcock

Your ideas, in the order you described them.

Notes from our conversation, organized into a roadmap a family could follow.

Sherene, I took notes while we talked, and afterward I tried to put what you described into an order a family could follow. This is what I came up with. It's your thinking, organized, and I want to know where I've got it wrong.

What's here

What you told me and what I noticed. Your story, as I'd hope to tell it with your permission. Your ideas organized as a nine-step Family Care Roadmap. The two kinds of family it serves. The line between what you do and what you'd never do. Then one question. The appendix holds the working briefs I drafted for each step; they're yours to keep.

Notes byRichard Ladson, Certified Medicaid Planner
ForSherene Woolcock, Senior Care Consultant
What I know about youWhat you told me, and what I noticed

What you told me, and what I noticed.

I'm starting from your words and what I've watched you do, not from a template.

Your goal

$10,000 a month

On top of what you do now. Not by finding more hours; you don't have them.

Your mission

To serve

Seniors and the families around them. You've held support groups for caregivers. You help people for free because that's who you are.

Your expertise

Memory care

Alzheimer's and dementia. Care plans, managing caregivers, what a good day looks like and what a bad night means. Plus the management experience to run it.

What I noticed

What you have

  • Ideas for a business you've carried for years.
  • Families already coming to you. That's demand, and it's the hardest thing to build.
  • A community you've already built, one support group at a time.
  • Your own story, with your father and your mother.

What's in the way

  • No written process, so every family starts from scratch and you're the only one who can help.
  • No pricing, so the help is free by default, and free doesn't scale or fund itself.
  • The business side, websites and software: work you don't enjoy and shouldn't have to do.

What I took from it

The generosity was never the problem. Without a structure it can reach one family at a time, and a structure is what would let it reach more. That's the thought behind the roadmap on the pages that follow.

Your storyThe reason families will trust you before they read a word

Your story is the front door.

Every family that finds you will want to know one thing before they read a checklist: does she understand what this is like? You do, and not from a textbook.

What I'd tell them, in your words, with your permission

You cared for your father. You've cared for your mother. You've sat in the chair every family caregiver sits in, the one where you're the daughter and the nurse and the scheduler at once, and you've run the support groups where caregivers say out loud what they can't say at home. Then you spent a career learning how care actually gets organized, delivered and managed. There is no one else with both halves of that.

Why I wrote it down

A family chooses a guide they believe has walked the road. Your story does that before you say a word, and the support groups you've hosted are the proof of it. I've put it near the front because, to me, it is the front.

The rule

Nothing about your family appears anywhere until you've written it yourself and said yes. This page is a placeholder for your words, not mine.

The roadmapYour ideas, organized

The Family Care Roadmap

When you talk about care there's an order in it: understand the person, then work out what good care looks like, then run it and hand it back to the family. Those are the three phases, with three steps in each. All of it comes from my notes of what you described, so correct anything.

PHASE 1 · ASSESS

Understand the person, the family, and the situation.

  1. 1
    DiscoverUnderstanding Your Family's Care SituationWrite down where things stand today, what has become hard, and what the family wants to protect.
  2. 2
    AssessUnderstanding Your Loved One's NeedsBuild a clear picture of health, daily function, safety, and the preferences a caregiver should know.
  3. 3
    Define NeedsCreating the Care Needs ProfileTurn what you've learned into the needs, risks, and priorities that point to the right level of care.

PHASE 2 · PLAN

Determine what good care should look like and prepare to put it in place.

  1. 4
    Explore OptionsChoosing the Right Type of CareCompare care settings and providers, and agree on how the family will make the decision.
  2. 5
    Build the PlanBuilding the Personal Care PlanSet down the health and personal care, the daily life worth preserving, and what to watch for.
  3. 6
    Prepare the TransitionPreparing for the TransitionGet ready for a move or a new caregiver so nothing important is lost along the way.

PHASE 3 · MANAGE

Coordinate the plan, review what happens, and prepare the family to take the lead.

  1. 7
    CoordinateCoordinating the Care TeamSettle who does what, how information is shared, and how the family works with the provider's plan.
  2. 8
    MonitorMonitoring and AdvocatingKnow what good care looks like, when to speak up, and how to keep the plan current.
  3. 9
    Hand OffTaking the LeadLearn the skills to manage care yourselves, with support when you need it.

Every step has a version for families who need care now and a version for families planning ahead; the next page explains the difference. The names on the steps are the first thing I'd expect you to change.

Two versionsNeed care now · Plan ahead

Two Versions of Every Step

Most families are deciding in a crisis; some have time to plan. So every step is drawn twice: once for the family in the middle of it, once for the family ahead of it. Not softer wording: different work, different completion.

Need Care Now

Care decisions, a transition, care-delivery concerns, or caregiver overload need attention now.

Understand the needs. Organize the plan. Coordinate the care.

Sherene helps families whose loved one needs care now understand the situation, organize a person-centered plan, and coordinate what happens next—without having to start every conversation from scratch, carry every task alone, or enter care meetings unprepared, even if the family is overwhelmed or unsure where to begin.

Plan Ahead

The family has time to document preferences, discuss roles, explore options, and prepare for changes.

Start the conversation. Prepare the family. Know when to act.

Sherene helps families prepare for an aging loved one’s changing care needs by documenting what matters, organizing a practical care roadmap, and preparing family roles and handoffs—without waiting for a crisis to start the conversation, assuming one person will handle everything, or making a placement decision before it is needed, even if their loved one is still largely independent.

The lineWhat you do · what you never do

Where the Line Is

The framework organizes care information and prepares the family. It does not replace a clinician's plan, and it does not touch money. I wrote these from what you said about where your work stops; correct me.

What you do

  • Care discovery, and assessment within your confirmed scope.
  • Care-plan preparation and provider-comparison support.
  • Transition coordination and care-plan meetings.
  • Family education, advocacy, and a practiced handoff.
  • Optional support after the handoff.

What you never do

  • Funding, Medi-Cal eligibility, insurance or asset planning.
  • Diagnose, prescribe, change medication, set clinical thresholds, or replace a provider's clinical plan.
  • Treat a relative's wishes as the person's own, or make activity attendance compulsory.
  • Call a course completion proof of a safe placement or a guaranteed result.
One questionDid I hear you right?

Did I hear you right?

That's the whole ask. Read it and tell me what's wrong, what's missing, and what you'd never say to a family.

What would help most

  • The names on the nine steps, and their order. Change anything.
  • What you're licensed or trained to assess, so every page that says “within scope” is true.
  • Anything I put in your mouth that you didn't say.

What happens next

Nothing, until you've reacted. If the roadmap holds up, there's more I'd like to show you about how I'd build around it, but that's a later conversation, and when to have it is your call.

Appendix A · BoundariesFrom the package

Boundaries

Service scopeSherene’s working lane is care discovery, assessment within confirmed scope, planning support, coordination, family education, advocacy, and handoff. Funding, Medicaid eligibility, insurance-funding, and asset planning are excluded.
Professional rolesThe curriculum organizes care information and prepares questions. It does not authorize families or AI to diagnose, prescribe, change medication, set clinical thresholds, or replace a provider’s clinical plan.
Person-centered careThe loved one’s stated preferences remain separate from family wishes. Activity support should preserve choice rather than require attendance.
Draft versus deliveryCourse completion produces an organized learner output. It is not proof of safe placement, a guaranteed care result, or confirmation that Sherene has accepted a professional engagement.
Unknowns and evidenceProvider availability, capabilities, information access, and the actual care-plan review schedule require case-specific confirmation. Missing evidence is not an on-plan status.
Unconfirmed business detailsSherene’s credentials, included meetings, service area, support cadence, response expectations, and directory/data access remain to be confirmed. No prices or financial projections are included.
Advertising statusAds are draft copy. No assertion is made about current ad-platform eligibility, approved targeting, conversion rates, or a live landing page. Claims and destinations need review before launch.
Appendix B · Service tiersFrom the package

Service tiers

High-touch: Sherene leads the coordinationPersonal family discovery and assessment within scope; care-plan preparation; provider-comparison support; transition coordination; explicitly included care-plan meetings; a practiced family handoff. Number of meetings and ongoing monitoring are not assumed.
Guided: Sherene teaches and reviewsThe family uses the same templates and courses with defined group coaching, office hours, or review support. Individual clinical questions are routed to the appropriate professional rather than answered by a generic group curriculum.
Self-directed: the family learns the processCourses, checklists, prompts, worksheets, and planning templates. Community access may be an optional addition. Self-study does not replace a professional assessment or create an ongoing care-management relationship.
Continuity: support after the handoffOptional scheduled check-ins, future meeting help, a moderated community, or periodic gatherings. Scope, cadence, coverage during absence, and response expectations must be agreed; no unlimited access is implied.
Appendix C · MetricsProposed, non-clinical

Proposed non-clinical metrics

MeasureQuestionHow it is recorded
Responsibility coverageWhich active coordination tasks have a confirmed owner and backup?Task table; confirmation date; not a clinical-quality score.
Open follow-upHow many agreed follow-up items are open or past their agreed date?Open, waiting, overdue, resolved; retain the source of the date.
Handoff completionWhich transfers have a recorded recipient acknowledgment?Sent, received, needs clarification, resolved.
Information freshnessWhen was the family plan or contact list last reviewed?Document version and last-reviewed date; no universal review interval assumed.
Caregiver capacityDoes the lead caregiver report that current responsibilities are manageable?A conversation prompt and agreed action, not a diagnostic burnout score.
Person’s experienceWhat does the person report about routines, choices, and meaningful activities?Use their words where possible; record offers and support without rewarding forced participation.
Care-plan follow-throughWhat is known about a small set of agreed care-plan items?Observed, reported, unknown, or needs follow-up, with source and date; clinical interpretation remains with professionals.

4 · Three struggles

6 · Million Dollar Message

Care Situation helps families facing an urgent care decision create one clear summary of the current care situation and the next decisions, without repeating the same story to different people, relying on scattered notes, or assuming someone else is handling an important task—even if nobody has organized the information before.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Record the event or change that created the immediate need.
  2. Confirm upcoming care decisions and any stated dates.
  3. Name a temporary family contact and a backup.

Working actions

  1. Document where the person lives and who provides help.
  2. Describe morning, daytime, evening, and overnight arrangements.
  3. List family members, professionals, and contact details.
  4. Record what each person actually does.
  5. Ask the primary caregiver which responsibilities are becoming difficult.
  6. Gather relevant existing care notes with appropriate permission.
  7. Separate confirmed facts, family observations, and unanswered questions.
  8. Review the summary with the loved one where possible and with the family.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The family and Sherene have a current summary, an identified contact, and a list of immediate decisions with unknowns clearly marked.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Start with the immediate decision
    • What triggered the request for help.
    • Which decision is next.
    • Who needs the situation summary today.
  2. Lesson 2 · Describe the situation
    • Separate current arrangements from proposed changes.
    • Describe a typical day rather than relying on broad labels.
    • Record what changed and when.
  3. Lesson 3 · Map the people and work
    • List family and professional caregivers.
    • Compare actual workload with assumed responsibilities.
    • Identify the person coordinating information.
  4. Lesson 4 · Build the starting summary
    • Combine notes without erasing disagreement.
    • Mark unknown information rather than filling gaps.
    • Prepare a focused review with Sherene.

14 · Prompt guide

5 AI Prompts for Care Situation — Need Care Now

Use only de-identified information you have permission to share. Treat AI as an organizer and drafting assistant, not as a clinician, a safety assessor, or a decision-maker for the person. Preserve unknowns, disagreements, and sources. Do not invent diagnoses, care orders, medication changes, clinical thresholds, provider capabilities, or legal authority. Flag decisions for the appropriate human professional. Do not use a prompt, course, or community channel as an urgent-help service.

  1. We need to address an active care situation now. Using only these notes [paste de-identified notes], help me organize our notes into a current-situation summary with a typical-day section. Mark missing information and decisions requiring human review. Give me an editable draft, not a clinical conclusion.
  2. We need to address an active care situation now. Using only these notes [paste de-identified notes], help me create an interview agenda that lets our loved one and the main caregiver speak. Mark missing information and decisions requiring human review. Give me an editable draft, not a clinical conclusion.
  3. We need to address an active care situation now. Using only these notes [paste de-identified notes], help me turn a list of caregiving tasks into a who-does-what table without assigning unwilling relatives. Mark missing information and decisions requiring human review. Give me an editable draft, not a clinical conclusion.
  4. We need to address an active care situation now. Using only these notes [paste de-identified notes], help me identify gaps or contradictions in the information without guessing which account is correct. Mark missing information and decisions requiring human review. Give me an editable draft, not a clinical conclusion.
  5. We need to address an active care situation now. Using only these notes [paste de-identified notes], help me draft a concise briefing for Sherene that distinguishes known facts from questions. Mark missing information and decisions requiring human review. Give me an editable draft, not a clinical conclusion.

2 · Currency · 3 · Outcome

CurrencyFocus
OutcomeIdentify the care problems that need attention and organize the conversations needed to address them.

4 · Three struggles

  • Trying to solve every disagreement at once.
  • Turning concerns into personal accusations.
  • Overlooking the caregiver who is running out of capacity.

5 · Three questions

  • What is actually going wrong?
  • Which responsibilities are not getting done?
  • What help does the primary caregiver need now?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Care Challenges helps families dealing with care breakdowns or caregiver overwhelm identify the care problems that need attention and organize the conversations needed to address them, without trying to solve every disagreement at once, turning concerns into personal accusations, or overlooking the caregiver who is running out of capacity—even if the family does not agree on the cause of the problem.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineToo Many Care Problems at Once?
Primary textA missed task, an overwhelmed caregiver, and an argument between siblings are different problems. A clear issue list helps the family discuss each one more constructively. Sort care concerns, family disagreements, and caregiver overload into a focused list of next actions.
BenefitLearn how to identify the care problems that need attention.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Care Problems Triage Worksheet
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. List current care gaps and upcoming decisions.
  2. Ask the primary caregiver what must change immediately.
  3. Identify concerns that need prompt attention from the responsible care professional.

Working actions

  1. Invite the loved one and family to name their main concerns.
  2. Write a concrete example for each concern.
  3. Record whether care, communication, paperwork, or workload is involved.
  4. Ask the lead caregiver which tasks cannot continue as they are.
  5. Document differing accounts without declaring a winner.
  6. Identify unresolved concerns needing professional attention.
  7. Select the concerns to discuss in the next family meeting.
  8. Assign a next action and follow-up owner for each selected issue.
  9. Keep an open-issues list rather than expecting one meeting to resolve everything.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The main concerns are documented with examples, caregiver capacity is visible, and each immediate issue has a next contact or action.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Focus the next conversation
    • Name the active problem.
    • Recognize overloaded caregivers.
    • Keep the discussion centered on the loved one’s needs.
  2. Lesson 2 · Name the actual problem
    • Replace broad complaints with specific examples.
    • Distinguish observations from interpretations.
    • Ask how the concern affects daily care.
  3. Lesson 3 · Include the caregiver and family
    • Make hidden workload visible.
    • Discuss unkept commitments without labeling relatives.
    • Notice conflict over a move or increased support.
  4. Lesson 4 · Prepare a useful conversation
    • Group related concerns.
    • State what needs clarification or help.
    • Refer concerns outside the service’s scope to the appropriate professional.

1 · Names

Short nameFamily Priorities

2 · Currency · 3 · Outcome

CurrencyAlignment
OutcomeCreate shared decision criteria while keeping the loved one’s wishes and unresolved disagreements visible.

4 · Three struggles

  • Assuming everyone wants the same outcome.
  • Letting the loudest voice define the plan.
  • Losing the person’s preferences in a rushed decision.

5 · Three questions

  • What does our loved one want?
  • Where does the family agree or disagree?
  • Which questions must be answered before we decide?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Family Priorities helps families making a difficult care decision create shared decision criteria while keeping the loved one’s wishes and unresolved disagreements visible, without assuming everyone wants the same outcome, letting the loudest voice define the plan, or losing the person’s preferences in a rushed decision—even if you cannot reach complete agreement today.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineHow Do You Choose When the Family Disagrees?
Primary textA difficult care decision is easier to discuss when the family can name what matters, what is disputed, and what still needs clarification. Start there rather than arguing over a solution. Bring your loved one’s wishes and the family’s concerns into the same care conversation.
BenefitPrepare a more focused family care conversation.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe What Matters Most Meeting Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Ask for the loved one’s current preferences.
  2. Name the decision that needs to be made.
  3. Document shared priorities and unresolved differences before comparing solutions.

Working actions

  1. Ask the loved one what matters most to them.
  2. Record routines and choices they want preserved.
  3. Ask each involved family member about concerns and desired outcomes.
  4. Separate the person’s wishes from the family’s preferences.
  5. Document where expectations conflict.
  6. Discuss what relatives can and cannot realistically provide.
  7. List questions requiring clinical or other professional clarification.
  8. Agree on criteria to use when comparing care options.
  9. Review the profile with the person where possible.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The profile separates the person’s wishes from family preferences and records decision criteria, unresolved issues, and who will clarify them.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Use priorities in an active decision
    • Keep the person’s voice visible.
    • Do not require artificial consensus.
    • Identify the information needed to move forward.
  2. Lesson 2 · Listen to the person receiving care
    • Ask what makes a good day.
    • Capture their own words when possible.
    • Do not replace their preferences with family assumptions.
  3. Lesson 3 · Listen to the family
    • Explore hopes and worries.
    • Separate preferences from available caregiving capacity.
    • Identify competing expectations.
  4. Lesson 4 · Create shared decision criteria
    • Record agreement and disagreement.
    • Identify tradeoffs for discussion.
    • Keep unresolved issues visible in the planning file.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Obtain the latest available care and discharge information.
  2. Document present abilities rather than only pre-hospital abilities.
  3. List clinical questions that must be clarified for the next arrangement.

Working actions

  1. Invite the loved one to describe what they can do and where help is useful.
  2. Record assistance with daily activities.
  3. Describe mobility and transfer support currently used.
  4. Gather current care instructions and relevant records.
  5. Record cognitive, emotional, and communication observations.
  6. Compile medication-management questions without changing medications.
  7. Record nutrition, swallowing, continence, and skin concerns for review.
  8. List therapies or services already involved.
  9. Arrange Sherene’s review within her confirmed professional scope.
  10. Route unresolved clinical questions to the responsible clinician.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

Current abilities, assistance, information sources, and open clinical questions are documented and assigned for professional review.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Assess the current picture
    • Notice recent changes.
    • Use current information.
    • Clarify what is not yet known.
  2. Lesson 2 · Describe everyday function
    • Discuss bathing, dressing, eating, toileting, and moving.
    • Record what the person does independently.
    • Describe assistance without treating a checklist as a diagnosis.
  3. Lesson 3 · Organize health-related information
    • Collect existing care instructions and medication information.
    • Record cognitive, emotional, nutrition, and communication concerns.
    • List questions for the appropriate clinician.
  4. Lesson 4 · Prepare the professional assessment
    • Compare family reports with the person’s account.
    • Identify information Sherene needs to confirm.
    • Maintain a source and date for observations.

CurrencyAwareness

4 · Three struggles

  • Assuming help will be available.
  • Overlooking overnight coverage.
  • Asking one caregiver to provide support they cannot sustain.

5 · Three questions

  • When will help be needed?
  • Who is actually available?
  • Which concerns need professional review before the transition?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Safety Support helps families arranging care after a recent change document immediate safety concerns, support gaps, and professional follow-up responsibilities, without assuming help will be available, overlooking overnight coverage, or asking one caregiver to provide support they cannot sustain—even if the family has not arranged replacement help yet.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineWill the Next Care Arrangement Have the Support It Needs?
Primary textA care plan needs more than a location. It also needs clear answers about assistance, supervision, backup coverage, and concerns that require professional review. Identify coverage gaps and questions the responsible professionals need to address before the arrangement changes.
BenefitReview the support questions before the next care transition.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Care Support Readiness Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Map support for the proposed next arrangement.
  2. Identify unfilled help or supervision periods.
  3. Take unresolved safety questions to the responsible care professional.

Working actions

  1. Document observed fall or mobility concerns.
  2. List times when supervision or help may be unavailable.
  3. Record medication-management difficulties for review.
  4. Identify environmental concerns reported or observed.
  5. Review the primary caregiver’s ability to provide the agreed help.
  6. Record relevant existing professional instructions.
  7. Identify missing backup coverage.
  8. Ask the appropriate professional to review unresolved safety questions.
  9. Record owners and follow-up for proposed changes.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

Current concerns and coverage gaps are visible, each has an owner, and unresolved safety questions have been referred rather than treated as cleared.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Review the proposed arrangement
    • Compare support needed with support available.
    • Check handoffs and overnight arrangements.
    • Do not equate a completed worksheet with safety clearance.
  2. Lesson 2 · Observe the environment and support
    • Document specific concerns rather than certify a home safe.
    • Identify when the person is alone.
    • Describe assistance currently available.
  3. Lesson 3 · Review coverage and caregiver capacity
    • Map daytime and overnight coverage.
    • Identify backup arrangements.
    • Include the caregiver’s practical limits.
  4. Lesson 4 · Create a professional follow-up list
    • Use existing instructions as the starting point.
    • Route clinical questions to the care team.
    • Record who will follow up on each concern.

4 · Three struggles

  • Losing familiar routines during admission.

5 · Three questions

  • What should new caregivers know about the person?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Personal Preferences helps families introducing a loved one to new caregivers create an About Me profile that carries the person’s daily preferences into the new care relationship, without relying on relatives to repeat every detail, losing familiar routines during admission, or substituting family wishes for the person’s own choices—even if important details have never been written down.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineWill the Care Team Know More Than a Diagnosis?
Primary textMorning tea, familiar activities, and how someone likes to be approached belong in the care conversation. An About Me profile helps the family share those details clearly. Put meaningful routines, communication preferences, and daily choices into an easy-to-share profile.

ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe About Me Handoff Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Ask which routines matter most during this transition.
  2. Prepare a concise profile for new caregivers.
  3. Confirm who will receive and review it.

Working actions

  1. Ask the person to describe a good day.
  2. Record preferred morning and evening routines.
  3. Document meal preferences and usual timing.
  4. Keep allergies and clinician-prescribed dietary instructions distinct from preferences.
  5. List meaningful activities and relationships.
  6. Describe communication approaches the person prefers.
  7. Ask what helps during an unfamiliar situation.
  8. Confirm the profile with the person where possible.
  9. Prepare a short version for authorized care-team sharing.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

A person-centered profile is confirmed where possible, preferences are distinguished from care orders, and a sharing recipient is identified.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Introduce the person to new caregivers
    • Choose immediately useful details.
    • Keep the profile readable.
    • Ask the receiving team to confirm receipt.
  2. Lesson 2 · Learn the person’s ordinary day
    • Ask open-ended questions.
    • Use their own words where possible.
    • Include familiar routines and relationships.
  3. Lesson 3 · Capture preferences accurately
    • Separate wishes from clinical instructions.
    • Record what support participation requires.
    • Notice disagreement between family assumptions and the person’s preferences.
  4. Lesson 4 · Create the About Me profile
    • Keep the staff-facing version easy to read.
    • Confirm what the person wants shared.
    • Plan how preferences can be updated.

Brief 3.1 · Care GapsNeed Care Now

3.1 Care Gaps · Need Care Now

Find the Gaps in Today’s Care. Compare what your loved one needs with the help actually in place.

Review status: Draft — Sherene review pending · Provenance: Framework and process mapping: current conversation. Asset copy and outline: new draft adaptation of uploaded production method.

1 · Names

Short nameCare Gaps
Course titleIdentifying Care Needs & Risks
This version's titleFind the Gaps in Today’s Care
Question headlineWhat Is Falling Through the Cracks?
How-to headlineHow to Find the Gaps in Today’s Care
General topicNeeds & Risks

2 · Currency · 3 · Outcome

CurrencyVisibility
OutcomeCreate a documented list of care gaps and the follow-up each one requires.

4 · Three struggles

  • Assuming a listed service is being delivered.
  • Confusing uncertainty with a confirmed failure.
  • Overlooking gaps covered informally by one exhausted relative.

5 · Three questions

  • Which needs are not being met?
  • What do we know and what still needs checking?
  • Who will address each gap?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Care Gaps helps families concerned that current care is not meeting identified needs create a documented list of care gaps and the follow-up each one requires, without assuming a listed service is being delivered, confusing uncertainty with a confirmed failure, or overlooking gaps covered informally by one exhausted relative—even if the available information is incomplete.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineWhat Is Falling Through the Cracks?
Primary textA useful care review compares the plan with the real arrangement. See which needs have support, which are uncertain, and which need a clear follow-up. Compare what your loved one needs with the help actually in place.
BenefitIdentify the gaps that need a care conversation.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Care Gaps Review Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Compare current needs with actual daily support.
  2. Verify unclear information with the appropriate source.
  3. Assign prompt follow-up to unresolved concerns.

Working actions

  1. Gather the family summary and assessment findings.
  2. List each documented support need.
  3. Identify what currently meets that need.
  4. Flag needs with no reliable support.
  5. Record conflicting or missing information.
  6. Include meaningful-activity and communication gaps.
  7. Identify where family commitments exceed capacity.
  8. Refer clinical uncertainty for professional review.
  9. Assign a next step for each unresolved gap.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

Each identified gap has a source, an owner, a status, and a next action or professional-review route.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Review the active arrangement
    • Work from current observations.
    • Check assumptions.
    • Make follow-up ownership explicit.
  2. Lesson 2 · Bring the assessment together
    • Combine person, family, and professional information.
    • Retain sources and uncertainties.
    • Avoid treating repeated statements as independent confirmation.
  3. Lesson 3 · Compare needs with actual support
    • Identify assistance already in place.
    • Make uncovered tasks visible.
    • Include caregiver capacity and meaningful daily life.
  4. Lesson 4 · Create an actionable gap register
    • State gaps neutrally.
    • Assign professional-review questions.
    • Prepare priorities for the roadmap.

11 · The deliverable the family completes

TitleCare Needs and Gaps Register
PurposeCreate a documented list of care gaps and the follow-up each one requires.

Fields:

  • Documented need
  • Source and date
  • Support currently provided
  • Gap or unresolved question
  • Impact described by the person or family
  • Professional review needed
  • Action owner
  • Status

Blank learner-output specification; not a completed assessment or plan for an actual family.

Working actions

    • Translate observations into questions about support.

    • List supervision and professional-service requirements.

    • Write needs-based criteria.
    • Get professional confirmation where required.
    • Carry the brief into provider research.

2 · Currency · 3 · Outcome

CurrencyPrioritization
OutcomeCreate a prioritized care roadmap with clear responsibilities and professional follow-up.

4 · Three struggles

  • Trying to do everything at once.
  • Taking steps before their prerequisites are resolved.
  • Leaving one relative to coordinate every task.

5 · Three questions

  • What should happen first?
  • Who is responsible?
  • What must be clarified before we act?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Care Roadmap helps families facing several immediate care decisions create a prioritized care roadmap with clear responsibilities and professional follow-up, without trying to do everything at once, taking steps before their prerequisites are resolved, or leaving one relative to coordinate every task—even if you do not yet have every answer.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineWhat Should the Family Do Next?
Primary textKnowing the concerns is not the same as knowing the next step. A written roadmap shows what comes first, who will do it, and which questions still need professional input. Turn assessments and open questions into an organized sequence of care actions.
BenefitOrganize your family’s next care steps.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Next Care Steps Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Identify the next decision and any confirmed deadline.
  2. Prioritize its prerequisites and professional questions.
  3. Assign owners and confirm what the lead caregiver can realistically handle.

Working actions

  1. Review assessment findings and unresolved questions.
  2. List decisions that need to be made.
  3. List actions needed before those decisions.
  4. Identify professional reviews and who will request them.
  5. Separate actions to do now, later, or when a trigger occurs.
  6. Assign a willing owner to each active task.
  7. Confirm backups for important responsibilities.
  8. Record agreed dates and dependencies.
  9. Check whether the primary caregiver’s workload is realistic.
  10. Share the roadmap with authorized participants.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The next actions are sequenced, owned, and dated where appropriate, and unresolved decisions have a clear review route.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Sequence urgent care work
    • Start with actual decision dates.
    • Identify prerequisites.
    • Do not let incomplete information disappear.
  2. Lesson 2 · Turn findings into actions
    • Translate concerns into specific next steps.
    • Distinguish decisions from tasks.
    • Keep professional-review items visible.
  3. Lesson 3 · Sequence the work
    • Identify dependencies.
    • Separate immediate action from monitoring.
    • Assign owners according to actual capacity.
  4. Lesson 4 · Create the shared roadmap
    • Record dates and follow-up.
    • Identify a backup for critical tasks.
    • Review the roadmap with participants.

  • Professional involvement

6 · Million Dollar Message

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineWhat Should You Ask Before Choosing a Provider?
Primary textAvailability is only one question. Families also need to ask about actual support, staffing coverage, daily routines, and the capabilities their loved one requires. Check capabilities, availability, and daily-care details instead of relying on a brochure alone.
BenefitGet the questions for a more focused provider search.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Care Provider Interview Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Identify requirements that must be confirmed before admission or service start.
  2. Contact providers about current availability.
  3. Record unresolved capability questions for immediate follow-up.

Working actions

  1. Create search criteria from the care requirements brief.
  2. Identify relevant providers through available resources.
  3. Contact providers to confirm current availability.
  4. Ask about private and shared room arrangements.
  5. Ask which staff provide support during each shift.
  6. Clarify nursing availability and what happens when a need exceeds routine coverage.
  7. Ask about required mobility, communication, and personal-care support.
  8. Ask about activities and help to participate.
  9. Clarify therapy coordination and changing-care arrangements.
  10. Record the source and date for each answer.
  11. Record inspection or other quality information separately from provider claims.
  12. List questions to verify during a tour or follow-up.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

Provider records include current sources, dates, capability questions, and unresolved items; no unverified entry is treated as an accepted placement.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Research for an active need
    • Verify availability directly.
    • Prioritize essential capability questions.
    • Track who provided each answer.
  2. Lesson 2 · Build the search criteria
    • Use essential requirements and preferences.
    • Include location and family access.
    • Avoid collecting information with no decision purpose.
  3. Lesson 3 · Ask providers specific questions
    • Ask about current availability.
    • Distinguish daytime and overnight coverage.
    • Ask how the person’s particular support needs would be addressed.
  4. Lesson 4 · Verify and document the findings
    • Record the source and date.
    • Separate provider statements from independent information.
    • Keep unknowns visible rather than assigning an unsupported rank.

  1. Confirm which options are genuinely available for the next arrangement.
  2. Resolve essential capability questions with the provider and relevant professionals.
  3. Record the decision, reasons, and remaining conditions.

Working actions

  1. Choose a manageable set of options that meet the preliminary criteria.
  2. Use consistent questions on tours or provider calls.
  3. Document observations and provider answers separately.
  4. Compare essential care capabilities.
  5. Discuss environment, preferences, and family access.
  6. Invite the loved one’s participation where possible.
  7. Document disagreement without implying a majority vote overrides the person.
  8. Identify the appropriate decision participant or representative for the situation.
  9. Record reasons for the choice or for deferring it.
  10. List any confirmations required before transition.
  11. Identify a backup path when feasible.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The appropriate decision participant has a documented comparison and decision, with remaining conditions and transition actions clearly identified.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Support the active decision
    • Compare current options.
    • Keep unresolved conditions explicit.
    • Move only the agreed decision into transition planning.
  2. Lesson 2 · Prepare the comparison
    • Use the same criteria for each option.
    • Separate essentials from preferences.
    • Avoid a score that hides missing information.
  3. Lesson 3 · Manage the family conversation
    • Let participants explain concerns.
    • Return to the person’s needs and wishes.
    • Distinguish a family contact from decision-making authority.
  4. Lesson 4 · Document the decision
    • Record tradeoffs and outstanding confirmations.
    • Identify the next action.
    • Retain a backup option where feasible.

6 · Million Dollar Message

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineIs the Daily Care Plan Clear Enough to Discuss?
Primary textA family care-plan proposal can make important details easier to discuss: daily assistance, existing instructions, preferences, and questions the clinical team still needs to answer. Bring assessed needs, existing instructions, and unanswered care questions together before the team meeting.

ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Personal Care Planning Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Collect the current assessment and professional instructions.
  2. Identify questions affecting present daily care.
  3. Prepare a review-ready proposal for the next care-team conversation.

Working actions

  1. Review documented care needs and current instructions.
  2. Organize mobility and transfer assistance information.
  3. Record hygiene and continence support needs.
  4. Document skin-related instructions already provided by professionals.
  5. List nutrition, hydration, and food-texture questions needing confirmation.
  6. Organize current medication-management responsibilities.
  7. Request a full medication review from the appropriate professional where indicated.
  8. Document therapy coordination needs.
  9. Keep preferences separate from clinical instructions.
  10. List questions for Sherene and the responsible care team.
  11. Mark the document as a proposal until relevant care decisions are confirmed.
  12. Record the plan’s author, date, and revision status.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The proposal is complete enough for review, sources and unresolved items are visible, and clinical decisions remain assigned to the appropriate professionals.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Prepare for the active care-plan meeting
    • Focus on current support.
    • Bring the latest instructions.
    • Keep the proposal separate from the provider’s authorized plan.
  2. Lesson 2 · Build from assessed needs
    • Use the care requirements brief.
    • Include day-to-day personal assistance.
    • Avoid copying instructions from another person’s plan.
  3. Lesson 3 · Separate orders, preferences, and questions
    • Record existing medication and treatment instructions accurately.
    • Keep family requests distinguishable.
    • Refer prescribing and clinical decisions for appropriate review.
  4. Lesson 4 · Prepare a review-ready plan
    • Identify who needs to confirm each section.
    • Record unresolved items.
    • Version the family proposal before care-team discussion.

Working actions

  1. Review the About Me profile.
  2. Ask the person what they want an ordinary day to include.
  3. List meaningful morning and evening routines.
  4. Document preferred meals and timing.
  5. Keep clinical dietary instructions separate from preferences.
  6. Identify activities the person enjoys.
  7. Describe help needed to participate, such as transport or reminders.
  8. Plan family contact and important relationships.
  9. Record how staff should offer choices and respond when the person declines.
  10. Discuss practical arrangements with the care team.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

A good-day proposal reflects the person’s preferences, describes practical support, and records what the care team has agreed to or still needs to discuss.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Improve the current daily experience
    • Start with the person’s feedback.
    • Discuss access to activities, not forced participation.
    • Confirm what can be supported.
  2. Lesson 2 · Define a good day with the person
    • Begin with their preferences.
    • Identify familiar activities and relationships.
    • Notice when relatives are guessing.
  3. Lesson 3 · Make preferences practical
    • Describe invitations, assistance, and timing.
    • Keep dietary instructions distinct.
    • Plan for choices to change from day to day.
  4. Lesson 4 · Discuss the plan with caregivers
    • Ask what can be accommodated.
    • Record agreed routines and unanswered questions.
    • Review enjoyment and choice, not attendance alone.

5.3 Care Monitoring · Need Care Now

Decide What to Monitor in the Current Care Plan. Set up a practical observation and follow-up process for the care arrangement already in place.

Review status: Draft — Sherene review pending · Provenance: Framework and process mapping: current conversation. Asset copy and outline: new draft adaptation of uploaded production method.

1 · Names

Short nameCare Monitoring
Course titleKnowing What to Watch For
This version's titleDecide What to Monitor in the Current Care Plan
Question headlineHow Will You Know Whether the Plan Is Happening?
How-to headlineHow to Decide What to Monitor in the Current Care Plan
General topicMonitoring & Response

2 · Currency · 3 · Outcome

CurrencyAwareness
OutcomeCreate a monitoring plan with defined observations, information sources, and response contacts.

4 · Three struggles

  • Tracking everything without a purpose.
  • Treating missing information as reassuring.
  • Collecting concerns without assigning follow-up.

5 · Three questions

  • Which care-plan items should we watch?
  • Who can provide reliable information?
  • Who should respond to a concern?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Care Monitoring helps families beginning oversight of a current care arrangement create a monitoring plan with defined observations, information sources, and response contacts, without tracking everything without a purpose, treating missing information as reassuring, or collecting concerns without assigning follow-up—even if you cannot be present every day.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineHow Will You Know Whether the Plan Is Happening?
Primary textA shared tracker should show what is known, what is unconfirmed, and what needs follow-up. Start with the care-plan items that matter—not a long list of numbers nobody reviews. Set up a practical observation and follow-up process for the care arrangement already in place.
BenefitBuild a practical care monitoring and response plan.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Care Monitoring Setup Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Select observations tied to the active plan.
  2. Confirm available information sources.
  3. Agree response contacts with the current care team.

Working actions

  1. Identify care-plan items worth monitoring.
  2. Choose a small starting set relevant to the person.
  3. Define what each observation means.
  4. Identify the information source and person recording it.
  5. Record a baseline when information is available.
  6. Use not observed or unknown when data is missing.
  7. Agree when routine review will occur.
  8. Ask clinicians to confirm clinical warning and response instructions.
  9. Identify the right contact for operational concerns.
  10. Assign follow-up responsibility.
  11. Review whether the monitoring workload is practical for the family.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

Each selected item has a definition, information source, owner, review process, and response route; missing evidence is explicitly marked.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Set up monitoring for active care
    • Use the current plan.
    • Respect limits on access and reporting.
    • Separate monitoring from emergency response.
  2. Lesson 2 · Choose useful observations
    • Connect each item to a care-plan goal.
    • Distinguish care delivery from clinical outcomes.
    • Avoid collecting measurements no one will review.
  3. Lesson 3 · Define evidence and ownership
    • Identify who actually has access to the information.
    • Keep family observations separate from provider documentation.
    • Use unknown when there is no evidence.
  4. Lesson 4 · Plan the response
    • Agree routine contacts and follow-up.
    • Have clinical response thresholds confirmed by clinicians.
    • Keep urgent-help routes separate from community or coaching access.

  • Unknown or not-observed status

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineWho Is Handling the Paperwork, Equipment, and Move?

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Confirm the planned transition and provider requirements.
  2. Assign owners to missing essential items.
  3. Review readiness with the people responsible for the transition.

Working actions

  1. Confirm the nature of the transition, including new caregivers at home when relevant.
  2. Request the receiving provider’s preparation requirements.
  3. Gather care records and current medication information.
  4. Prepare the personal profile and care-plan proposal.
  5. Confirm equipment and supply requirements with the relevant professionals.
  6. Create a belongings list.
  7. Identify transport arrangements appropriate to the person’s needs.
  8. Assign each preparation task and a backup.
  9. Discuss the transition with the loved one where possible.
  10. Record missing items and who will resolve them.
  11. Check the lead caregiver’s workload.
  12. Prepare a final pre-transition review.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

Required preparation items are assembled or explicitly outstanding, owners are confirmed, and the team can see whether any essential issue still needs resolution.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Prepare for an actual transition
    • Use the confirmed requirements.
    • Track outstanding items.
    • Avoid treating a checklist as clinical clearance.

    • Ask the receiving provider what is required.
    • Keep care paperwork separate from out-of-scope financial or legal work.

    • Assign willing owners and backups.

    • Confirm receipt of requested information.
    • Escalate missing essential items to the responsible team.
    • Prepare the admission-day checklist.

HeadlineWhat Should You Check When Care Begins?

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Confirm the current admission or service-start arrangements.
  2. Document the receiving contacts and handoffs.
  3. Create a dated follow-up list for unresolved transition questions.

Working actions

  1. Confirm arrival or service-start arrangements.
  2. Identify the receiving staff contact.
  3. Bring the agreed care information packet.
  4. Confirm who received medication and care instructions.
  5. Check that agreed equipment and supplies have a confirmed responsible party.
  6. Identify the correct contact for routine and urgent concerns.
  7. Record immediate discrepancies and who will resolve them.
  8. Ask the person about comfort and adjustment where possible.
  9. Confirm arrangements for the first care-plan discussion.
  10. Share an update with authorized family participants.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The transition log identifies received information, contacts, unresolved concerns, and the next care-plan discussion; unresolved issues are not treated as complete.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Manage the live transition
    • Use actual arrival information.
    • Record discrepancies promptly.
    • Assign the next follow-up.
  2. Lesson 2 · Understand the transition day
    • Confirm practical arrangements with the provider.
    • Identify the family’s primary contact.
    • Prepare the person and their familiar belongings.
  3. Lesson 3 · Check the first handoffs
    • Confirm receipt of care information.
    • Ask who handles immediate questions.
    • Document discrepancies rather than assuming they were resolved.
  4. Lesson 4 · Organize the first-days follow-up
    • Record concerns and responses.
    • Ask about the care-plan meeting process.
    • Review adjustment with the person and caregivers.

8 · The working checklist

Working actions

  1. Identify the sending and receiving contacts.
  2. Gather the current care information and its sources.
  3. Include the About Me profile.
  4. Include the family care-plan proposal with its review status.
  5. List open questions and outstanding records.
  6. Confirm appropriate permission for sharing.
  7. Record what is transmitted and when.

9 · Definition of done

Transferred items, receipt, and outstanding clarifications are recorded with owners; sending alone is not treated as completion.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Close the current transfer loop
    • Reconcile what arrived.
    • Confirm important updates.
    • Keep unresolved items visible.
  2. Lesson 2 · Decide what must travel
    • Include current care information and personal preferences.
    • Keep clinical instructions accurately sourced.
    • Include unresolved questions rather than hiding them.
  3. Lesson 3 · Make the handoff explicit
    • Identify the receiving person.
    • Record what was sent.
    • Ask for confirmation of receipt and the next review step.
  4. Lesson 4 · Close the information loop
    • Compare what was sent with what was received.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Create the packet from current confirmed information.
  2. Assign a person to maintain its version and review date.
  3. Prepare a receipt log for future use rather than claiming a handoff has occurred.

Working actions

  1. Identify the sending and receiving contacts.
  2. Gather the current care information and its sources.
  3. Include the About Me profile.
  4. Include the family care-plan proposal with its review status.
  5. List open questions and outstanding records.
  6. Confirm appropriate permission for sharing.
  7. Record what is transmitted and when.
  8. Confirm receipt with the receiving contact.
  9. Assign follow-up for missing or unclear items.
  10. Check that updated information reaches the relevant care team.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

A current packet, maintenance owner, and future receipt-confirmation process exist; no transfer is marked complete before it occurs.

    • Include current care information and personal preferences.
    • Keep clinical instructions accurately sourced.
    • Include unresolved questions rather than hiding them.
  3. Lesson 3 · Make the handoff explicit
    • Identify the receiving person.
    • Record what was sent.
    • Ask for confirmation of receipt and the next review step.
  4. Lesson 4 · Close the information loop
    • Compare what was sent with what was received.
    • Resolve missing or conflicting information through the appropriate team.
    • Keep a versioned packet.

2 · Currency · 3 · Outcome

CurrencyOwnership
OutcomeCreate a confirmed team plan with realistic family responsibilities and professional contact routes.

4 · Three struggles

  • Assuming someone else owns a task.
  • Confusing a family coordinator with a clinical decision-maker.
  • Leaving all follow-up to one overwhelmed person.

5 · Three questions

  • Who handles each task?
  • Who is the backup?
  • Which questions belong with Sherene and which with a clinician?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Care Team helps families coordinating an active care arrangement create a confirmed team plan with realistic family responsibilities and professional contact routes, without assuming someone else owns a task, confusing a family coordinator with a clinical decision-maker, or leaving all follow-up to one overwhelmed person—even if responsibilities have grown informally over time.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineWho Is Actually Responsible for Each Care Task?
Primary textA list of names is not yet a care team plan. Connect each responsibility to an owner, a backup, and the right professional contact—and check that the workload is realistic. Clarify roles, contacts, and backups so important work does not fall between people.
BenefitCreate a clearer who-does-what care plan.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Care Team Responsibilities Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Identify current tasks without an owner.
  2. Confirm family and professional contacts.
  3. Redistribute work that the primary caregiver cannot sustain.

Working actions

  1. List family and professional participants.
  2. Ask the loved one whom they want involved where possible.
  3. Document the established healthcare representative or flag uncertainty for clarification.
  4. Separate that role from the routine family contact.
  5. List recurring tasks and decisions.
  6. Assign willing owners according to capacity.
  7. Assign backup responsibility for critical coordination tasks.
  8. Identify the clinician responsible for medication and treatment questions.
  9. Define Sherene’s agreed coordination responsibilities.
  10. Review the primary caregiver’s workload.
  11. Confirm how participants contact one another.
  12. Share the plan only with appropriate permission and access.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

Active tasks have confirmed owners, professional boundaries and contacts are clear, and gaps in family capacity have a follow-up plan.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Clarify today’s responsibility gaps
    • Resolve unowned tasks.
    • Confirm existing commitments.
    • Address overloaded coordination.
  2. Lesson 2 · Map the whole team
    • Include the person receiving care.
    • List family and professional participants.
    • Separate coordination from clinical decision-making.
  3. Lesson 3 · Assign work realistically
    • Ask who can actually take a task.
    • Include nearby and distant family contributions.
    • Name backups for important responsibilities.
  4. Lesson 4 · Check that the plan can operate
    • Confirm contact routes.
    • Identify authority questions needing appropriate review.
    • Test what happens when the usual coordinator is unavailable.

4 · Three struggles

  • Assuming a message reached the right person.
  • Repeating updates without recording decisions.

5 · Three questions

  • Who needs this information?
  • Who owns the next action?
  • How will we know the handoff was received?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Care Handoffs helps families struggling with fragmented care communication establish a repeatable handoff process for changes, open tasks, and follow-up, without assuming a message reached the right person, repeating updates without recording decisions, or letting responsibility disappear between caregivers—even if the family and care team use different communication channels.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineDoes the Next Person Know What Needs to Happen?
Primary textA useful handoff tells the next person what changed, what remains open, and what they need to do. Use a simple format across the family and the provider’s agreed channels. Create clear updates and ownership for care information moving between people.
BenefitCreate clearer care handoffs and follow-up.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Care Handoff Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Identify a recent communication breakdown.
  2. Agree sender, receiver, and channel for that type of update.
  3. Record ownership and acknowledgment for the next live handoff.

Working actions

  1. Identify the handoffs that recur in the care arrangement.
  2. Ask the provider which channels and contacts the family should use.
  3. Agree a family update channel.
  4. Create a brief handoff format.
  5. Identify sender and receiver.
  6. Include relevant changes and open tasks.
  7. Specify who owns the next action.
  8. Request acknowledgment when needed.
  9. Record unconfirmed or unanswered handoffs.
  10. Review how backup caregivers receive the current information.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The agreed protocol is used for an actual handoff and any missing acknowledgment or ownership is recorded for follow-up.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Repair a live handoff
    • Use a real recent example.
    • Respect the provider’s communication process.
    • Confirm the next action rather than only sending a message.
  2. Lesson 2 · Define what needs a handoff
    • Focus on changes, decisions, and unfinished work.
    • Use the agreed provider communication channels.
    • Include family-to-family transitions.
  3. Lesson 3 · Use a repeatable message
    • State what happened and what is needed.
    • Name a receiver and owner.
    • Make the request specific enough to answer.
  4. Lesson 4 · Close the loop
    • Record acknowledgment.
    • Follow up if ownership is unclear.
    • Update the shared action log.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Choose a family communication channel and current-plan location.
  2. Draft a standard handoff format.
  3. Rehearse a coordinator absence using a fictional or de-identified example.

Working actions

  1. Identify the handoffs that recur in the care arrangement.
  2. Ask the provider which channels and contacts the family should use.
  3. Agree a family update channel.
  4. Create a brief handoff format.
  5. Identify sender and receiver.
  6. Include relevant changes and open tasks.
  7. Specify who owns the next action.
  8. Request acknowledgment when needed.
  9. Record unconfirmed or unanswered handoffs.
  10. Review how backup caregivers receive the current information.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The protocol, shared-plan location, and backup handoff have been rehearsed, with gaps recorded and assigned for correction.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Practice before a real absence
    • Choose a realistic scenario.
    • Test access as well as understanding.
    • Fix the information gaps the rehearsal exposes.
  2. Lesson 2 · Define what needs a handoff
    • Focus on changes, decisions, and unfinished work.
    • Use the agreed provider communication channels.
    • Include family-to-family transitions.
  3. Lesson 3 · Use a repeatable message
    • State what happened and what is needed.
    • Name a receiver and owner.
    • Make the request specific enough to answer.
  4. Lesson 4 · Close the loop
    • Record acknowledgment.
    • Follow up if ownership is unclear.
    • Update the shared action log.

2 · Currency · 3 · Outcome

CurrencyAgreement
OutcomeComplete an alignment record showing agreed actions and unresolved differences between family priorities and the provider plan.

4 · Three struggles

  • Assuming a request became part of the plan.
  • Leaving the meeting without owners or follow-up.
  • Treating every disagreement as a personal conflict.

5 · Three questions

  • Where are our priorities reflected?
  • What has actually been agreed?
  • Who will follow up on unresolved items?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Plan Alignment helps families preparing for a current provider care-plan meeting complete an alignment record showing agreed actions and unresolved differences between family priorities and the provider plan, without assuming a request became part of the plan, leaving the meeting without owners or follow-up, or treating every disagreement as a personal conflict—even if you have never attended a care-plan meeting.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineDoes Everyone Understand the Same Care Plan?
Primary textBring more than a list of concerns. Bring the family’s priorities, the current care information, and a way to record what was agreed, what remains open, and who will act next. Prepare the questions and priorities that need a documented answer from the care team.
BenefitPrepare for a more useful care-plan meeting.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Care-Plan Meeting Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Confirm the next actual care-plan meeting.
  2. Compare current priorities with the available provider plan.
  3. Prepare a meeting record with action and decision fields.

Working actions

  1. Obtain the care-plan meeting arrangements from the provider.
  2. Confirm Sherene’s attendance under the agreed service scope.
  3. Prepare the family’s priority questions.
  4. Bring the current personal care proposal and About Me profile.
  5. Ask how those priorities appear in the provider’s plan.
  6. Discuss differences and practical constraints.
  7. Record clinical questions for the appropriate professional.
  8. Identify which requests were accepted, deferred, or declined.
  9. Ask how agreed changes will be documented and communicated.
  10. Assign action owners and follow-up.
  11. Send an appropriate summary to the family.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The meeting record distinguishes agreed actions from requests, assigns follow-up, and identifies how the provider will confirm relevant plan changes.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Prepare for an active care-team discussion
    • Use the latest plan version.
    • Focus on the family’s highest-priority questions.
    • Record decisions and follow-up clearly.
  2. Lesson 2 · Prepare for the meeting
    • Bring the current family proposal and profile.
    • Identify the most important questions.
    • Clarify who will speak and take notes.
  3. Lesson 3 · Discuss differences constructively
    • Compare needs, routines, and provider arrangements.
    • Ask for explanation where plans differ.
    • Keep clinical decisions with the responsible professionals.
  4. Lesson 4 · Document what was agreed
    • Separate requests from accepted actions.
    • Assign owners and follow-up.
    • Confirm how changes enter the provider’s plan.

2 · Currency · 3 · Outcome

CurrencyVisibility
OutcomeComplete a care review showing confirmed observations, information gaps, and assigned follow-up.

4 · Three struggles

  • Relying on a vague feeling that things are fine.
  • Treating missing observations as proof of good or poor care.
  • Collecting concerns without checking what was actually agreed.

5 · Three questions

  • What did the plan say would happen?
  • What information do we have?
  • What needs follow-up?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Care Review helps families overseeing an active care arrangement complete a care review showing confirmed observations, information gaps, and assigned follow-up, without relying on a vague feeling that things are fine, treating missing observations as proof of good or poor care, or collecting concerns without checking what was actually agreed—even if you are not at the facility or home every day.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineHow Do You Check Whether the Care Plan Is Happening?
Primary textCare oversight starts with a comparison: what was agreed, what is known, and what remains unconfirmed. A simple review makes the next conversation more specific. Use dated observations and specific questions rather than impressions alone.
BenefitLearn a practical way to review the care plan.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Care Delivery Review Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Use the current agreed care plan.
  2. Review a defined recent period with available observations.
  3. Assign follow-up to discrepancies and missing information.

Working actions

  1. Select the current care-plan items under review.
  2. Record the agreed expectation for each.
  3. Gather available family observations.
  4. Request appropriate information through agreed provider channels.
  5. Record source and date.
  6. Ask about the person’s experience where possible.
  7. Mark unknown or not observed items clearly.
  8. Identify discrepancies and unanswered questions.
  9. Assign follow-up owners.
  10. Review whether the observation workload is sustainable.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The review identifies its period, sources, known information, unknowns, and action owners without making unsupported clinical conclusions.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Conduct a current care review
    • Use dated information.
    • Separate evidence from impressions.
    • Make follow-up practical.
  2. Lesson 2 · Review against the agreed plan
    • Use specific agreed items.
    • Distinguish expectations from assumptions.
    • Include the person’s feedback.
  3. Lesson 3 · Record useful evidence
    • Label direct observations and provider reports.
    • Mark missing evidence as unknown.
    • Do not treat a dashboard as a clinical assessment.
  4. Lesson 4 · Turn findings into follow-up
    • Identify discrepancies for discussion.
    • Track response and resolution.
    • Review the family’s monitoring workload.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Create a review template using a practice scenario.
  2. Identify potential observers and reviewers.
  3. List the information-access questions to confirm with future providers.

Working actions

  1. Select the current care-plan items under review.
  2. Record the agreed expectation for each.
  3. Gather available family observations.
  4. Request appropriate information through agreed provider channels.
  5. Record source and date.
  6. Ask about the person’s experience where possible.
  7. Mark unknown or not observed items clearly.
  8. Identify discrepancies and unanswered questions.
  9. Assign follow-up owners.
  10. Review whether the observation workload is sustainable.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The family has a rehearsed review template, provisional roles, and explicit future access and expectation questions.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Practice a review before implementation
    • Use a clearly labeled example.
    • Avoid claiming access that is not arranged.
    • Identify who will maintain the review.
  2. Lesson 2 · Review against the agreed plan
    • Use specific agreed items.
    • Distinguish expectations from assumptions.
    • Include the person’s feedback.
  3. Lesson 3 · Record useful evidence
    • Label direct observations and provider reports.
    • Mark missing evidence as unknown.
    • Do not treat a dashboard as a clinical assessment.
  4. Lesson 4 · Turn findings into follow-up
    • Identify discrepancies for discussion.
    • Track response and resolution.
    • Review the family’s monitoring workload.

2 · Currency · 3 · Outcome

CurrencyVoice
OutcomePrepare and document a clear care-concern conversation with an appropriate follow-up route.

4 · Three struggles

  • Letting frustration replace specific examples.
  • Repeating a complaint without asking for a clear response.
  • Allowing an unresolved issue to lose its follow-up owner.

5 · Three questions

  • What should we say?
  • Whom should we contact?
  • What happens if the issue remains unresolved?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Care Advocacy helps families facing an unresolved care or coordination concern prepare and document a clear care-concern conversation with an appropriate follow-up route, without letting frustration replace specific examples, repeating a complaint without asking for a clear response, or allowing an unresolved issue to lose its follow-up owner—even if you are worried about creating conflict.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineHow Do You Raise a Care Concern Clearly?
Primary textSpeaking up does not have to begin with an accusation. State what was observed, ask for clarification, and record the action and follow-up the conversation produces. Prepare a factual conversation, document the response, and keep follow-up moving.
BenefitPrepare a clearer care-concern conversation.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Speak-Up Preparation Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Identify the current concern and any need for immediate professional help.
  2. Choose the appropriate contact for the issue.
  3. Prepare the factual request and follow-up record.

Working actions

  1. Record the specific concern and available facts.
  2. Identify whether the issue is care delivery, communication, family workload, or a clinical question.
  3. Use the appropriate immediate-help route when the situation cannot wait.
  4. Identify the correct routine contact for non-urgent concerns.
  5. Prepare a clear question or request.
  6. Document the response.
  7. Agree who owns follow-up and when it will occur.
  8. Escalate unresolved issues through appropriate channels.
  9. Keep the person’s perspective visible.
  10. Refer entrenched conflict or issues beyond Sherene’s agreed scope to suitable outside support.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The concern has been communicated through an appropriate route and its response, owner, and next step are documented; unresolved concerns remain open.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Address a real concern
    • Choose the right route.
    • State facts and a clear request.
    • Track the response rather than assuming resolution.
  2. Lesson 2 · Describe the concern clearly
    • Use observations and dates.
    • Explain the care-plan connection.
    • Avoid blaming or diagnosing.
  3. Lesson 3 · Have the conversation
    • Make a clear request.
    • Listen to the response.
    • Keep family disagreements distinct from clinical questions.
  4. Lesson 4 · Follow through appropriately
    • Record the response and commitment.
    • Use agreed escalation contacts for unresolved issues.
    • Do not wait for group coaching when immediate professional help is needed.

Three priority actions
