Working actions

  1. Identify new information or a planned review point.
  2. Record changes in the person’s needs or preferences.
  3. Review changes in caregiver availability.
  4. Identify affected sections of the plan.
  5. Prepare questions for Sherene and the appropriate care professionals.
  6. Confirm the actual provider review process and schedule.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Review an active change
    • Use current observations.
    • Ask for appropriate review.
    • Avoid treating a pending proposal as an approved change.
  2. Lesson 2 · Recognize reasons to review
    • Include changes in functioning, preferences, and family capacity.
    • Use confirmed observations.
    • Do not assume every change requires a move.
  3. Lesson 3 · Prepare the review
    • Compare the current plan with new information.
    • Identify questions for the responsible professionals.
    • Keep family and provider documents distinct.
  4. Lesson 4 · Document and communicate updates
    • Record the decision and who authorized relevant changes.
    • Version the family document.
    • Confirm that affected people receive the update.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Identify tasks Sherene currently performs.
  2. Rehearse those the family plans to take over.
  3. Document remaining support needs before agreeing the handoff.

Working actions

  1. Review the current care plan and supporting documents.
  2. Identify who will lead family coordination.
  3. Teach document access and version control.
  4. Practice the routine care-review checklist.
  5. Practice preparing for a care meeting.
  6. Practice documenting a concern and identifying the right contact.
  7. Review family roles and backups.
  8. Ask the family to explain the process in its own words.
  9. Record tasks that still need Sherene’s support.
  10. Agree which coordination responsibilities are ready to transfer.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The lead and backup can locate the plan and demonstrate agreed oversight tasks, while unsupported tasks remain explicitly assigned rather than silently transferred.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Prepare for an actual service handoff
    • Practice live coordination examples.
    • Check both lead and backup.
    • Transfer only agreed responsibilities.
  2. Lesson 2 · Understand the operating routine
    • Locate the current documents.
    • Understand recurring tasks.
    • Keep provider duties distinct from family oversight.
  3. Lesson 3 · Practice the key skills
    • Prepare a meeting agenda.
    • Record a concern and follow-up.
    • Explain how to contact the right professional.
  4. Lesson 4 · Review readiness for handoff
    • Ask the family to demonstrate the process.
    • Identify gaps without treating course attendance as competence.
    • Agree which responsibilities can transfer.

HeadlineHow Do You Ask for Better Support and Follow Through?
Primary textEffective advocacy includes asking clearly, listening, documenting the response, and following up. StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Choose a current care or workload issue.
  2. Prepare and rehearse a specific request.
  3. Record the commitment or unresolved disagreement and its follow-up.

Working actions

  1. Review the loved one’s current priorities.
  2. Choose an advocacy situation to practice.
  3. Prepare a factual observation and clear request.
  4. Practice listening and clarifying the response.
  5. Create a family discussion process for disagreements.
  6. Practice asking another relative for a specific contribution.
  7. Record commitments and follow-up.
  8. Discuss the lead caregiver’s limits and need for breaks.
  9. Identify issues requiring outside facilitation or professional help.
  10. Review what the family can now handle independently.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The family has practiced a relevant advocacy conversation and can document requests, commitments, limits, and when outside help is needed.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Apply advocacy to today’s responsibilities
    • Use a real concern.
    • Ask for achievable commitments.
    • Keep unresolved conflict visible.
  2. Lesson 2 · Advocate from the person’s priorities
    • Distinguish advocacy from controlling every decision.
    • Use observations and specific requests.
    • Keep the person’s voice visible.
  3. Lesson 3 · Manage difficult family conversations
    • Discuss workload and limits.
    • Ask for realistic commitments.
    • Do not promise to resolve entrenched conflict through a checklist.
  4. Lesson 4 · Follow through collaboratively
    • Document what was agreed.
    • Check whether commitments were completed.
    • Seek outside help when the issue exceeds the family’s or Sherene’s role.

4 · Three struggles

6 · Million Dollar Message

Family Advocacy helps families preparing for future care conversations create a family discussion agreement and practice advocacy and workload-sharing skills, without avoiding disagreement until a crisis, assuming asking for help is a failure, or expecting one relative to become the permanent care coordinator—even if relatives have different communication styles.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineHow Will Your Family Talk About Care When Opinions Differ?
Primary textFamilies do not need identical opinions to prepare a useful conversation process. Practice clear requests, realistic commitments, and a way to seek help when the discussion stalls. Agree communication habits and practice asking for help before responsibilities increase.
BenefitPrepare for calmer, clearer family care conversations.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Family Care Conversation Readiness Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Discuss how the family wants to communicate.
  2. Practice a hypothetical disagreement about responsibilities.
  3. Agree how commitments and unresolved concerns will be recorded.

Working actions

  1. Review the loved one’s current priorities.
  2. Choose an advocacy situation to practice.
  3. Prepare a factual observation and clear request.
  4. Practice listening and clarifying the response.
  5. Create a family discussion process for disagreements.
  6. Practice asking another relative for a specific contribution.
  7. Record commitments and follow-up.
  8. Discuss the lead caregiver’s limits and need for breaks.
  9. Identify issues requiring outside facilitation or professional help.
  10. Review what the family can now handle independently.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

A discussion agreement and practice record exist, with clear ways to ask for help, record commitments, and seek outside support.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Build the communication habit early
    • Use low-pressure practice.
    • Normalize limits and backup support.
    • Avoid promising conflict-free care.
  2. Lesson 2 · Advocate from the person’s priorities
    • Distinguish advocacy from controlling every decision.
    • Use observations and specific requests.
    • Keep the person’s voice visible.
  3. Lesson 3 · Manage difficult family conversations
    • Discuss workload and limits.
    • Ask for realistic commitments.
    • Do not promise to resolve entrenched conflict through a checklist.
  4. Lesson 4 · Follow through collaboratively
    • Document what was agreed.
    • Check whether commitments were completed.
    • Seek outside help when the issue exceeds the family’s or Sherene’s role.

9.3 Ongoing Support · Need Care Now

Complete the Handoff with the Right Support. Confirm family responsibilities, remaining support, and the circumstances that call for renewed help.

How-to headlineHow to Complete the Handoff with the Right Support

2 · Currency · 3 · Outcome

CurrencyContinuity
OutcomeComplete an agreed handoff and support plan with clear responsibilities and re-engagement routes.

4 · Three struggles

  • Ending support without checking readiness.
  • Assuming someone is always available.
  • Leaving the family unsure when to seek help again.

5 · Three questions

  • What are we taking over?
  • What support continues?
  • When should we bring Sherene or another professional back in?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Ongoing Support helps families moving from Sherene-led coordination to family-led oversight complete an agreed handoff and support plan with clear responsibilities and re-engagement routes, without ending support without checking readiness, assuming someone is always available, or leaving the family unsure when to seek help again—even if you want some support rather than a complete step-away.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineWhat Happens After Sherene Steps Back?
Primary textA handoff does not have to mean being left alone. Define what the family will manage, what support is actually included, and whom to contact when the situation changes. Confirm family responsibilities, remaining support, and the circumstances that call for renewed help.
BenefitPlan a clear handoff and the support that follows.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Handoff and Support Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Confirm demonstrated readiness for the agreed transferred tasks.
  2. Choose a defined ongoing support arrangement or independent-management path.
  3. Record open items, contact expectations, and re-engagement triggers.

Working actions

  1. Review the family’s demonstrated coordination skills.
  2. List exactly which responsibilities are transferring.
  3. Keep unresolved tasks assigned.
  4. Confirm the family lead and backup.
  5. Discuss whether periodic Sherene check-ins are desired.
  6. Discuss future care-meeting support where available.
  7. Clarify any group or community support being considered.
  8. Confirm scope and contact expectations before service commitments are made.
  9. Record re-engagement triggers.
  10. Keep urgent professional help separate from coaching or community access.
  11. Agree a handoff review date.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The family and Sherene have an agreed responsibility transfer, explicit support terms still subject to service confirmation, and clear routes for unresolved or new concerns.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Complete an actual coordination handoff
    • Confirm readiness and agreement.
    • Record what remains with professionals.
    • Avoid open-ended availability promises.
  2. Lesson 2 · Define the handoff
    • List what is transferring.
    • Confirm the family’s readiness and consent.
    • Keep clinical care and provider responsibilities in place.
  3. Lesson 3 · Choose ongoing support
    • Discuss desired check-ins and meeting help.
    • Treat community and coaching as optional defined services.
    • Confirm availability and response expectations before promising them.
  4. Lesson 4 · Plan for re-engagement
    • Identify changes that warrant fresh help.
    • Know which professional fits which issue.
    • Test continuity when Sherene or the family coordinator is unavailable.
